title: Tasks and await
summary: What a Task is, how await gets the value out of it, why async spreads up the call chain, and how Sidekick saves your data without blocking.

steps.title: Waiting without blocking
body: A database query or an API call spends almost all of its time **waiting**: the request is out on the network and your program has nothing to do.

If the code simply stops and waits, its thread is **blocked**. It is held, but doing nothing. A web server that blocks one thread per request runs out of threads. A desktop app that blocks its main thread freezes.

Think of a waiter. A bad waiter takes one order, then stands at the kitchen door until the food is ready. A good waiter hands in the order, gets a ticket, and serves other tables until the kitchen calls.
In C# the ticket is a **`Task`**:
- `Task` is work in progress that will finish at some point.
- `Task<T>` is work in progress that will finish **and produce a `T`**. A `Task<int>` is not an `int`. It is the promise of one.
Methods that return a task are called **asynchronous**. By convention their names end in `Async`: `ReadAllTextAsync`, `SaveChangesAsync`, `GetStringAsync`.

steps.prompt: Match each piece to what it means.
pairs: work in progress, with no result value
work in progress that will produce a `decimal`

steps.title: async and await
body: **`await`** is how you get the value out of a task.
```csharp
static async Task<int> GetStockAsync(string sku)
await Task.Delay(20);        // stands in for a real database call
return 12;
int stock = await GetStockAsync("TEA");
Console.WriteLine(stock);        // 12
- `await someTask` means: *pause this method here until the task is finished, and let the thread go do other work meanwhile.* When the task finishes, the method carries on from that line.
- `await` **unwraps** the task. Awaiting a `Task<int>` gives you an `int`. Awaiting a plain `Task` gives you nothing; it just waits.
- A method may only use `await` if it is marked **`async`**, and an `async` method returns `Task` or `Task<T>`.
- Inside `async Task<int>` you `return` a plain `int`. The compiler wraps it in the task for you.
`Task.Delay(20)` is a task that finishes after 20 milliseconds. This course uses it as a stand-in for real I/O.
At the top level of a program you can use `await` directly, as in the example.

steps.prompt: Complete the method and the call.
steps.explain: The method produces a string later, so it returns `Task<string>`. `await` pauses until the delay is over. Awaiting the `Task<string>` unwraps it, so `name` is a plain `string`.
With `await` on every call, async code reads top to bottom just like ordinary code. The difference is invisible here: during the 10 ms delay, no thread is blocked.

steps.title: Async all the way
body: Once one method is async, the methods that call it become async too.
```csharp
static async Task<string> LoadNameAsync(int userId) { ... }
static async Task<string> GetGreetingAsync(int userId)
string name = await LoadNameAsync(userId);   // needs await...
return $"Hello, {name}";                      // ...so this method is async too
static async Task ShowGreetingAsync(int userId)   // Task: finishes, but has no result
Console.WriteLine(await GetGreetingAsync(userId));

To use the result you have to `await`. To `await` you have to be `async`. So `async` climbs the call chain until it reaches the top: your top-level statements, a web framework, or a test runner, which all know how to await.
This is normal and expected. It is called **async all the way**. Do not try to stop the chain halfway by forcing the result out of a task; a later lesson shows why that goes wrong.
A method with nothing to return uses `async Task`, the async version of `void`.

steps.prompt: Arrange the lines into an async method that loads a user's name and returns a greeting.
steps.explain: The name has to be awaited before it can be used in the greeting. The method returns a plain `string`; `async` wraps it into the `Task<string>`.

steps.prompt: `GetCountAsync` is declared as `static async Task<int> GetCountAsync()`. What happens with this line?
options: It does not compile: a `Task<int>` cannot be stored in an `int`
It works, and waits for the count
It works, and `count` is `0` until the task finishes
It compiles, but throws an exception when it runs
steps.explain: Without `await` you are holding the ticket, not the meal. The compiler will not turn a `Task<int>` into an `int` for you. Write `int count = await GetCountAsync();`.

steps.title: Where Sidekick keeps your data
body: Until now Sidekick forgot everything when it exited. This lesson's piece fixes that: it saves your tasks and time entries as JSON in **your user folder**, in `%USERPROFILE%\.sidekick\sidekick.json` (on your machine that is something like `C:\Users\you\.sidekick`).
```csharp
string home = Environment.GetFolderPath(Environment.SpecialFolder.UserProfile);
string root = Path.Combine(home, ".sidekick");        // never glue paths with "\" yourself
File work is I/O, so it has async versions that do not block a thread while the disk works:
```csharp
await using (var stream = File.Create(temp))                  // await using: an async Dispose
await JsonSerializer.SerializeAsync(stream, snapshot, options);
File.Move(temp, path, overwrite: true);                       // swap the finished file into place
await using var input = File.OpenRead(path);
var back = await JsonSerializer.DeserializeAsync<Snapshot>(input, options);
Two habits from real apps:
- **Write to a temporary file, then move it over the real one.** If the program dies halfway through writing, your old data is still there instead of half a JSON file.

- **Take the folder as a parameter** (`new JsonFileStore(root)`). The real `sk` passes `%USERPROFILE%\.sidekick`; the tests pass a scratch folder of their own. Same code, no risk to your real data. That parameter is called a *seam*.

steps.title: Build an invoice
prompt: The tests provide a fake shop database:
```csharp
record Order(int Id, int CustomerId, int Total);
static class Shop
public static Task<Order> GetOrderAsync(int orderId);
public static Task<string> GetCustomerNameAsync(int customerId);
Write two methods:
- `static async Task<string> BuildInvoiceAsync(int orderId)`
Loads the order, then the name of its customer, and returns text like `Invoice 7 for Maya: 120`.
- `static async Task AppendInvoiceAsync(int orderId, List<string> invoices)`
Builds the invoice for that order and adds it to the `invoices` list. It returns no value.

static async Task AppendInvoiceAsync(int orderId, List<string> invoices)
solution: static async Task AppendInvoiceAsync(int orderId, List<string> invoices)
template: Dojo.Eq("AppendInvoiceAsync adds finished invoices to the list", new List<string> { "Invoice 7 for Maya: 120", "Invoice 9 for Maya: 30" }, invoices);

public static async Task<Order> GetOrderAsync(int orderId)

`AppendInvoiceAsync` awaits `BuildInvoiceAsync(orderId)` and calls `invoices.Add(...)` with the result. An `async Task` method needs no `return`.

steps.title: Sidekick remembers
prompt: **Sidekick piece: the file store.** After this, `sk add`, `sk start` and `sk done` survive between runs.
The tests give you your `TaskItem` (from Robust code), `TimeEntry` (from Objects and types) and the two records `sk` saves:
```csharp
record TaskData(int Id, string Title, int EstimateMinutes, int LoggedMinutes, bool Done,
string? Tag, string? Project, DateOnly? Due, DateTime? RunningSince);
record Snapshot(List<TaskData> Tasks, List<TimeEntry> Entries);
Write:
1. `static TaskData ToData(TaskItem task)`: copy the fields. `RunningSince` is `task.StartedAt` while the timer runs, otherwise `null`.

2. `static TaskItem FromData(TaskData data)`: the reverse. Build the task with its constructor and set `Tag`, `Project`, `Due`; then `Log` the minutes (only when more than 0), `Start` the timer when `RunningSince` has a value, and `Complete` it when `Done`.
3. `class JsonFileStore` with
- a constructor `JsonFileStore(string root)` and a `Root` property,
- `FilePath`: `Path.Combine(Root, "sidekick.json")`,
- `async Task SaveAsync(Snapshot snapshot)`: create the folder, serialize (indented) to `FilePath + ".tmp"`, then move it over `FilePath`,
- `async Task<Snapshot> LoadAsync()`: when there is no file, an empty `Snapshot` (two empty lists); otherwise the deserialized snapshot.
`using System.Text.Json;` is already in place. Write the two methods first, then the class.
starter: return new Snapshot(new List<TaskData>(), new List<TimeEntry>());
solution: task.Tag, task.Project, task.Due, task.IsRunning ? task.StartedAt : null);
var task = new TaskItem(data.Id, data.Title, data.EstimateMinutes) { Tag = data.Tag, Project = data.Project, Due = data.Due };
static readonly JsonSerializerOptions Options = new() { WriteIndented = true };
if (!File.Exists(FilePath)) return new Snapshot(new List<TaskData>(), new List<TimeEntry>());

Dojo.Eq("ToData copies every field", new TaskData(3, "Fix login", 45, 20, false, "bug", "web", dojoDue, null), ToData(dojoTask));
Dojo.Eq("ToData of a running task keeps when it started", (DateTime?)new DateTime(2026, 11, 25, 9, 0, 0), ToData(dojoRunning).RunningSince);
var dojoBack = FromData(new TaskData(7, "Ship it", 30, 50, false, "chore", "core", dojoDue, null));
Dojo.Eq("FromData restores the title", "Ship it", dojoBack.Title);
Dojo.Eq("FromData restores tag, project and due", "chore core 2026-11-30", $"{dojoBack.Tag} {dojoBack.Project} {dojoBack.Due:yyyy-MM-dd}");
var dojoResumed = FromData(new TaskData(8, "Timer", 0, 0, false, null, null, null, new DateTime(2026, 11, 25, 8, 15, 0)));
Dojo.Check("FromData restarts a running timer", dojoResumed.IsRunning && dojoResumed.StartedAt == new DateTime(2026, 11, 25, 8, 15, 0), "IsRunning should be true with StartedAt 08:15");
Dojo.Check("FromData restores a finished task", FromData(new TaskData(9, "Old", 0, 10, true, null, null, null, null)).Done, "Done should be true");
Dojo.Eq("FilePath is sidekick.json inside the root", Path.Combine(dojoRoot, "sidekick.json"), dojoStore.FilePath);
await Dojo.TryAsync("LoadAsync with no file yet", async () =>
Dojo.Eq("LoadAsync with no file gives an empty snapshot", "0 tasks, 0 entries", $"{empty.Tasks.Count} tasks, {empty.Entries.Count} entries");
new List<TimeEntry> { new(3, new DateTime(2026, 11, 24, 9, 0, 0), new DateTime(2026, 11, 24, 9, 20, 0)) });
Dojo.Check("SaveAsync creates the folder and the file", File.Exists(dojoStore.FilePath), "no file at " + dojoStore.FilePath);
Dojo.Check("SaveAsync leaves no .tmp file behind", !File.Exists(dojoStore.FilePath + ".tmp"), "the temporary file was not moved into place");
Dojo.Eq("a new store on the same folder loads the same tasks", dojoSnapshot.Tasks, again.Tasks);
Dojo.Eq("and the same time entries", dojoSnapshot.Entries, again.Entries);
await dojoStore.SaveAsync(new Snapshot(new List<TaskData> { ToData(dojoTask) }, new List<TimeEntry>()));
Dojo.Eq("saving again replaces the file", 1, (await dojoStore.LoadAsync()).Tasks.Count);
public TaskItem(int id, string title, int estimateMinutes = 0)
if (id < 1) throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(id), "Task ids start at 1.");
if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(title)) throw new ArgumentException("A task needs a title.", nameof(title));
if (estimateMinutes < 0) throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(estimateMinutes), "An estimate cannot be negative.");
public int LoggedMinutes { get; private set; }
public bool IsRunning { get; private set; }
public DateTime StartedAt { get; private set; }
public bool Done { get; private set; }
string projectPart = Project is { Length: > 0 } p ? $" @{p}" : "";
string duePart = Due is DateOnly d ? $" (due {d:ddd d MMM})" : "";
if (Done) throw new InvalidOperationException("A finished task cannot be started.");
if (at < StartedAt) throw new ArgumentException("A timer cannot stop before it started.", nameof(at));
if (minutes < 1) throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(minutes), "Log at least one minute.");
enum Status { Todo, Doing, Blocked, Done }
record TimeEntry(int TaskId, DateTime Start, DateTime End)
public static bool CanMove(Status from, Status to) => (from, to) switch
(Status.Doing, Status.Todo or Status.Blocked or Status.Done) => true,
record TaskData(int Id, string Title, int EstimateMinutes, int LoggedMinutes, bool Done,
string? Tag, string? Project, DateOnly? Due, DateTime? RunningSince);

require.message: Moves the finished temporary file into place

hints: `ToData` is one `new(...)` with the fields in the record's order; for the last one: `task.IsRunning ? task.StartedAt : null`.

`SaveAsync`: `Directory.CreateDirectory(Root);` then `await using (var stream = File.Create(temp)) await JsonSerializer.SerializeAsync(stream, snapshot, options);` then `File.Move(temp, FilePath, overwrite: true);`.

`LoadAsync`: `if (!File.Exists(FilePath)) return new Snapshot(new List<TaskData>(), new List<TimeEntry>());` then `await using var stream = File.OpenRead(FilePath);` and `return await JsonSerializer.DeserializeAsync<Snapshot>(stream, options) ?? <empty>;`.
steps.explain: Your `sk` now loads `sidekick.json` when it starts and saves it when a command changed something. Delete the file and Sidekick starts fresh; copy it and you have a backup. Run `sk add "Try the store"` twice in your Code space: the second run says it is already on your list.
